section.title: The Whole World Accountable
section.sectionRationale: Paul answers the objections his argument has raised. What advantage has the Jew? Much, for they were entrusted with the very words of God. Does human unfaithfulness cancel God's faithfulness? Never; let God be true and every man a liar. Then Paul gathers a chain of Old Testament texts to prove the universal charge: none is righteous, no not one. The law speaks so that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God, for by works of the law no one will be justified; through the law comes only the knowledge of sin.
section.thesis: God remains faithful and just even though every human being is a liar, and Scripture itself testifies that Jew and Greek alike are wholly under sin; therefore the law cannot justify anyone but instead silences every excuse and exposes the guilt of the whole world before God.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the real advantage of the Jew and the unshakable faithfulness of God despite human unbelief; the catena of Scripture proving that no one is righteous; and the verdict that every mouth is stopped and no one is justified by works of the law, which only brings knowledge of sin.

units.label: God remains faithful and true
units.note: the advantage of the Jew, though every man a liar

verses.text: What, then, is the advantage of being a Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision?
Much in every way. First of all, they have been entrusted with the very {{logion|words}} of God.
What if some did not have faith? Will their lack of faith nullify God's {{pistis|faithfulness}}?
Certainly not! Let God be true and every man a liar. As it is written: “So that You may be proved right when You speak and victorious when You judge.”
But if our unrighteousness highlights the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unjust to inflict His wrath on us? I am speaking in human terms.
Certainly not! In that case, how could God judge the world?
However, if my falsehood accentuates God's truthfulness, to the increase of His glory, why am I still condemned as a sinner?
Why not say, as some slanderously claim that we say, “Let us do evil that good may result”? Their condemnation is deserved!

units.label: None is righteous, no not one
units.note: the verdict of Scripture on the whole race

verses.text: What then? Are we any better? Not at all. For we have already made the charge that Jews and Greeks alike are all under {{hamartia|sin}}.
As it is written: “There is no one {{dikaios|righteous}}, not even one.
There is no one who understands, no one who seeks God.
All have turned away, they have together become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one.”
“Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit.” “The venom of vipers is on their lips.”
“Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness.”
“Their feet are swift to shed blood;
ruin and misery lie in their wake,
and the way of peace they have not known.”
“There is no fear of God before their eyes.”

units.label: Every mouth stopped, the whole world accountable
units.note: no one justified by works of the law

verses.text: Now we know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God.
Therefore no one will be {{dikaioo|justified}} in His sight by works of the law. For the law merely brings awareness of sin.

logion.gloss: An oracle or divine utterance, the very words of God. Paul names Israel's chief advantage: they were entrusted with God's own revelation, the Scriptures. This is a stewardship, not a possession to boast in; being given the oracles of God magnifies both the privilege and the responsibility, and makes disbelief the more serious.

pistis.gloss: Faith or faithfulness. Here it names God's faithfulness, His covenant reliability, which human unbelief cannot cancel. The same word runs through the letter for the faith that receives God's righteousness; God's faithfulness and our faith belong to the one story of a God who keeps His word though every man prove false.

hamartia.gloss: Sin, a missing of the mark, understood by Paul not merely as scattered wrong acts but as a power that holds people captive. To be under sin is to be under its dominion and its guilt. Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin, which is why the whole world stands accountable and needs a rescue from outside itself.

dikaios.gloss: Righteous, just, in right standing before God. The catena opens with the verdict there is no one righteous, not even one. No human being measures up to God's standard; the universal negative prepares for the good news that righteousness must come as a gift, not an achievement, through faith in Christ.

dikaioo.gloss: To justify, to declare righteous, a courtroom verdict of acquittal and right standing. Paul states the negative that governs the whole argument: no one will be justified by works of the law. The verb sets up the great positive of 3:21 following, that God justifies freely by grace through faith in Christ.

basic.context: Having shown that both the openly wicked and the religiously privileged stand condemned, Paul pauses to field objections. If the Jew is just as accountable, what advantage remains? And if human sin only shows off God's righteousness, is God unfair to judge? Paul answers, then delivers the summary of his whole indictment: a string of Scriptures proving that the entire human race is under sin.
basic.hermeneutics: The first half is diatribe, a rapid exchange of questions and answers with an imagined objector. The second half is a catena, a chain of Old Testament quotations woven together from the Psalms and Isaiah. Read the quotations as Paul's scriptural jury: he is not inventing a harsh verdict but showing that Israel's own Scriptures already pronounce the whole world guilty.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel's advantage is that they were entrusted with the logion, the oracles of God. Human unbelief cannot cancel God's pistis, His faithfulness. The charge is that all are under hamartia, sin as a ruling power. Scripture declares there is no one dikaios, righteous. And the conclusion follows: no one will be dikaioo, justified, by works of the law, which only brings knowledge of sin.
basic.typology: The words of God entrusted to Israel are the Scriptures that testify beforehand to Christ. The universal indictment recalls the flood generation and the tower of Babel, humanity together turned away, now shown to be the condition of every heart. The stopped mouth before God anticipates every knee bowing before the Judge.
basic.christ: Christ is the hidden answer to this passage. The whole point of proving universal guilt is to show that no one can be saved by the law, so that the righteousness of God in Christ, revealed in the very next verses, is the only hope. God's faithfulness, which no human unbelief can nullify, is kept supremely in sending His Son. The stopped mouth of the guilty is opened again only in Christ to confess and give thanks.
basic.god: God is faithful, true, and just. His reliability does not depend on human faith; though every person proves a liar, God stands proved right. He is the righteous Judge of all the world, and His judgment is entirely fair. He cannot be charged with injustice for punishing sin, and He will not be manipulated by the twisted logic that we should sin so grace may abound.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 51:4 stands behind verse 4, that God is proved right when He judges. Psalms 14 and 53, 5, 140, 10, 36, and Isaiah 59 supply the catena of verses 10 to 18. Galatians 2:16 restates that no one is justified by works of the law. Romans 3:23 sums it up: all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
basic.oneStory: The Bible's storyline of human rebellion, running from Eden through the flood and Babel and Israel's own failures, is here gathered into one verdict: none is righteous, no not one. Every mouth is stopped and the whole world is guilty before God. This is the darkness against which the gospel shines, for the very next word is but now, the announcement of a righteousness from God given freely in Christ.

context.literary:
Romans 3:1-20 is the closing movement of an indictment that began at 1:18, and it has three distinct parts that should be kept apart. Verses 1 to 8 are a rapid exchange of questions and answers. Paul has just said that circumcision is worthless without obedience, and he lets an objector push the point to its limit. If the Jew has no advantage, what was the covenant for? If human sin makes God's righteousness shine more brightly, why does He punish it? Each objection ends with Paul's sharp 'Certainly not!' The Greek, me genoito, is literally 'may it not be,' and it is the exclamation he uses at each point of danger through the letter, as at 6:2 and 6:15 and 7:7.

Verses 9 to 18 turn from conversation to Scripture. They are a chain of quotations from the Psalms, Ecclesiastes and Isaiah, woven into one portrait and arranged by parts of the body: the throat, tongue, lips and mouth in verses 13 and 14, the feet in verses 15 to 17, the eyes in verse 18. Verses 10 to 12 state the general verdict, and the rest shows how it is carried out. The picture begins with a mind that does not understand, moves to the speech, then to the walk, and ends with the eyes that do not look to God. Sin is described as a whole person, from the inside out.

Verses 19 and 20 are the courtroom conclusion. The jury has heard the evidence, and the verdict is delivered with a drumroll of universal words: 'every mouth,' 'the whole world,' 'no one.' The tone of the whole section shifts at the last clause, 'the law merely brings awareness of sin.' It is a bleak sentence, and it is also a door, for the next words are 'But now,' Romans 3:21.

The unit as a whole answers the question that Paul asked in chapter 1, whether anyone can stand. The structure is deliberately exhaustive: the pagan in chapter 1, the moralist in chapter 2 and the Jew in 2:17 to 29 are all shown guilty, and chapter 3 gathers them with Scripture itself as the witness.
context.historical:
The objections of verses 1 to 8 are likely those Paul heard in his actual ministry. Rumors followed him that he taught Jews to forsake Moses, Acts 21:21, and verse 8 says plainly that 'some slanderously claim' he teaches 'Let us do evil that good may result.' Paul is answering real accusations that were repeated in the synagogues and in the cities where he preached. The first hearers in Rome, many of them with a Jewish background, would also have felt the weight of the first question. If Jew and Gentile are equally under sin, then what was the point of Israel's election?

Israel had been given a unique place. Moses had told the people that no other nation had a god so near, or laws so righteous, Deuteronomy 4:7-8, and a psalmist says God 'declares His word to Jacob... He has done this for no other nation,' Psalm 147:19-20. Paul will return to this list in Romans 9:4-5, where he names the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the temple worship and the promises. In 3:2 he gives only the first, and he lets it carry the weight: they were 'entrusted with the very words of God.'

The Scripture chain is also a historical choice. The first century Jewish world knew the Psalms well. They were sung in worship and read in the synagogue. Paul quotes psalms that Israelites sang about the wicked, and he applies them to everyone, including the singers. Psalm 14 itself speaks of 'the sons of men,' not only the Gentile. Israel's own songbook carries a verdict on humanity that Israel had often directed at others.

Paul was writing from Corinth, around AD 57, and the city's courts were nearby. The language of charge, defense, verdict and accountable parties would be heard in the setting of a Roman lawcourt, and the last verses describe a defendant who has no speech left.
context.canonical:
Each element of the catena has its own setting, and Paul gathers them with care. Psalms 14 and 53 are nearly identical and describe the fool who says there is no God, with the LORD looking down 'to see if any understand, if any seek God,' Psalm 14:2. Psalm 5:9 speaks of throats like open graves, and Psalm 140:3 of the venom of vipers on the lips. Psalm 10:7 describes a mouth full of cursing and deceit. Isaiah 59:7-8 says the feet are swift to shed blood and the way of peace has not been known, and Psalm 36:1 closes with 'There is no fear of God before his eyes.' Ecclesiastes 7:20 supplies a general summary: 'Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.'

The context of these passages matters. Psalm 14 ends with a prayer, 'Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion!' Isaiah 59 describes the same sin and then says the LORD saw that there was no one to intercede and 'His own arm brought salvation,' Isaiah 59:16, and promises 'The Redeemer will come to Zion,' 59:20. Paul quotes that chapter for the diagnosis and will quote the next lines for the cure, in Romans 11:26. The catena is not despair cut off from hope. Each text points toward a rescue that God Himself provides.

The answer to the objection about God's righteousness comes from Psalm 51:4. David's confession followed Nathan's confrontation, 2 Samuel 12, and he says that God is 'proved right when You speak and blameless when You judge.' Paul's claim that God must be vindicated even when human beings fail is a conclusion that David reached on his knees. The rest of the Old Testament supports it. 'God is not a man, that He should lie,' Numbers 23:19, and in Isaiah 5:3-4 God Himself invites the people to judge between Him and His vineyard, asking 'What more could I have done for My vineyard than I already did for it?'

In the New Testament the verdict of verse 20 is repeated in Galatians 2:16 and 3:10 and drawn out in 3:22, where 'the Scripture pronounces all things confined by sin.' The same Psalm that Paul has just used to say that no one seeks God is quoted again in the line that Paul borrows for verse 20, Psalm 143:2, 'no one alive is righteous before You.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul writes to complete a case. He has spent two and a half chapters showing that the pagan, the moralist and the Jew are all guilty, and he now wants to answer the objections that rise when a Jewish reader hears this and to lock the argument with the weight of Scripture. He has three aims in this section.

The first is to guard God's character. In answering the questions in verses 1 to 8, Paul protects two things at once: the faithfulness of God to His promises, and the justice of God in judging. The Jew who hears that he is under sin might conclude that God has gone back on His word. Paul says the opposite is true: God's faithfulness is the fixed point, and human failure cannot move it.

The second is to leave no escape. By quoting the Psalms and Isaiah, Paul answers a Jewish reader who might say that the condemnation fits Gentiles only. These are Israel's own Scriptures, and they speak of 'the sons of men.' The verdict is written in the book the Jew loves best. Paul wants the reader to feel the weight of his own Scriptures against him.

The third is to prepare for grace. The 'But now' of verse 21 can only be heard rightly after the silence of verse 19. Paul's aim is not despair. He wants his readers to stop pleading their own case, so that they can receive a righteousness they did not make. The law, he says, brings awareness of sin, and that awareness is useful, for it is the beginning of the cure.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage is a description of the human condition set out with a purpose. It would be a mistake to treat verses 10 to 18 as a statement that every person commits every sin on the list, or that people are as bad as they could be. They are a portrait of what sin does to the human being, and they apply to each person in some measure. It would also be a mistake to turn the catena into a weapon against others. Paul's own 'we' in verse 9 includes him: 'Are we any better?'

What the passage prescribes, in effect, is silence before God. 'Every mouth may be silenced' is a description of what the law does, and it is also a stance that a person can take now. Anyone who begins a prayer by defending himself has not yet heard verse 19. The proper beginning for prayer is the one the tax collector used, 'God, be merciful to me, a sinner,' Luke 18:13.

The objections of verses 5 to 8 also carry a practical warning. The slander that grace encourages sin is a standing temptation, and it is not only an opponent's slander. Believers can speak and live as if sin were harmless because grace will cover it. Paul's reply here is brief, 'Their condemnation is deserved,' and he will give the long answer in chapter 6. The passage also tells the church to value the Scriptures that God has entrusted to it, and to read them as a word that judges first and saves after.

debates.question: Does universal sinfulness in verses 10 to 18 mean no one ever does any relative good?

views.label: Total inability, not that every act is as evil as possible
views.case: The historic Reformed reading holds that sin has reached every part of a person, so that no one is righteous before God, understands, or seeks Him, as Paul writes. This does not deny that unbelievers can do acts of kindness, justice and courage that benefit others. It says that none of these makes a person acceptable to God, and that none flows from a heart that seeks Him for His own sake.

views.label: Strong prophetic generalization
views.case: Some read the catena as the language of the psalmists, who speak of the wicked in sweeping terms while the same psalms speak of the righteous. Psalm 14:5 itself says 'God is in the company of the righteous.' On this view Paul gathers texts about the wicked and applies them to the situation of all people before God, stressing the corporate verdict.

views.label: A claim about standing, not about conduct
views.case: Others emphasize Paul's courtroom vocabulary. 'Righteous' here means acquitted before God's tribunal, and in that sense no one qualifies. This view is compatible with the other two and focuses on the question of what is required for a favorable verdict.

debates.bearing: All three views support the conclusion of verse 20: by works of the law no one will be justified. They differ in how they describe the moral condition of those who do not know Christ. Paul himself acknowledges a conscience that sometimes does the right thing, Romans 2:14-15, so the denial in verse 12 is of righteousness before God and not of every good act. The 'no one seeks God' also sits next to texts about seekers such as Acts 17:27, where God's design is that people would seek Him, and the Bible reconciles them by saying that He first moves, John 6:44.

debates.question: What are the 'works of the law' in verse 20?

views.label: Anything done to earn a right standing with God
views.case: The traditional Protestant reading takes the phrase to mean obedience to the whole law as a way of earning favor. Paul's argument from 1:18 has been about moral failure, including theft and adultery, and 3:20 follows the argument about doing good and evil. Galatians 3:10-12 says that the law requires doing everything written in it.

views.label: Jewish boundary markers
views.case: Scholars in the New Perspective on Paul argue that the phrase refers chiefly to the practices that marked Israel out from the nations, circumcision, Sabbath and food laws. On this reading Paul's concern is that Jews were treating those marks as proof of belonging, which is the theme of 2:17 to 29.

views.label: The whole law, including its identity markers
views.case: A third approach holds that the phrase means the law as a whole, with the boundary markers as its most visible part. Paul's point is that neither the identity markers nor the moral commands can justify a person, because the law cannot give life, Galatians 3:21.

debates.bearing: The context of verses 9 to 20 is about sin and not only about ethnic boundaries, since the quotations speak of violence, deceit and cursing. That favors a broad reading. Even so, the discussion of circumcision in chapter 2 and of the Jew's advantage in 3:1 shows that the markers are part of the target. Paul's point stands on either view: no performance, whether moral or ritual, gives a person a righteous standing.

debates.question: What does 'the faithfulness of God' mean in verse 3, and whose unfaithfulness is meant?

views.label: God's covenant faithfulness against Israel's unbelief
views.case: The question is whether the unbelief of some Israelites cancels God's promises. Paul answers that it does not. This is the majority view, and it explains why the argument returns to the question in chapters 9 to 11.

views.label: Unfaithfulness in general, not only unbelief in the gospel
views.case: The Greek word can mean either 'did not believe' or 'were unfaithful.' Some argue that Paul has in mind Israel's covenant infidelity across history, which fits the quotation from Psalm 51 about David's sin.

debates.bearing: The two readings largely coincide, because unbelief toward God's word is itself a form of unfaithfulness. What matters is Paul's insistence that the promise of God does not depend on the human response in order to remain true.

study.originalLanguages:
Verses 2 and 3 are held together by a family of words that share a root, which the English cannot keep. The Jews 'have been entrusted,' episteuthesan, with the words of God. Some 'did not have faith,' ēpistēsan, which can also mean they were unfaithful. And their lack of faith, apistia, cannot nullify the 'faithfulness,' pistis, of God. Four words from one stem, trust and entrusting and betrayal and faithfulness, are lined up on the page. Israel was trusted with a treasure, and some betrayed the trust, and God's own fidelity is the one thing that stands.

What Israel was entrusted with is the logia, the 'oracles' or 'utterances' of God. The Greek Old Testament uses the word for the sayings of the LORD that are 'flawless, like silver refined in a furnace,' Psalm 12:6. Stephen uses it of the 'living words' Moses received at Sinai, Acts 7:38. Paul chooses a word that means weighty utterances, not only commands, so the gift includes the promises as well as the law.

The great answer 'Certainly not!' in verses 4 and 6 is me genoito, a formula of horror used again and again through Romans. Verse 4 then says 'Let God be true and every man a liar.' The verb 'be true' is ginestho, 'let him be found,' and it speaks of what is shown at the end of an examination. The human liar is a quotation from Psalm 116:11, 'All men are liars.' The Psalm 51 quotation in verse 4 reads 'victorious when You judge.' Paul's Greek here, nikēsēs en tō krinesthai se, is the form of the Greek Old Testament, where the verb can be read either 'when You judge' or 'when You are judged.' The ambiguity fits the setting. God is placed on trial by the objector's question, and wins. The Hebrew psalm has 'blameless,' which the BSB uses in Psalm 51:4, and Paul's 'victorious' stresses the legal outcome.

In verse 5 God is said to 'inflict' wrath. The Greek participle is epipherōn, 'bringing on,' and the phrase 'I am speaking in human terms,' kata anthropon legō, is Paul's way of saying he is voicing an objection he finds absurd. Verse 8 speaks of those who 'slanderously claim,' blasphemoumetha, from the same family as the 'blasphemed' name of 2:24. The slander against the gospel and the blasphemy of the name are two forms of the same offense.

In verse 9 the question 'Are we any better?' translates a rare verb, proechometha, that translators divide over, rendering it 'Are we better off?' or 'Do we have any advantage?' or 'Are we worse off?' The sense is clear from Paul's answer, 'Not at all.' The word for 'charge,' proētiasametha, belongs to the lawcourt: Paul has 'already brought the charge.' The place where all sit is 'under sin,' hyph' hamartian. The preposition suggests being under a power, as in Romans 7:14, 'sold as a slave to sin,' and in Galatians 3:22 the Scripture 'confined' all things under it. Hamartia is used in the singular here for sin as a master, not only as a series of acts.

The verdict in verse 10, 'no one righteous,' uses dikaios, the same word family as the righteousness that will be revealed in verse 21. It is the word for one who has been vindicated by the court. The catena's repeated 'not even one,' ouk estin heos henos, closes every exit.

Verse 19 says every mouth 'may be silenced,' phragē, 'stopped' or 'shut.' It is the verb Hebrews 11:33 uses for shutting the mouths of lions. Paul pictures an accused person who is stopped by the evidence. 'Held accountable,' hypodikos, is a courtroom word meaning answerable to a judgment, and it describes a world standing in the dock.

Finally, 'justified' in verse 20 is dikaiothesetai, the verb of declaring someone in the right. In the Law, God says, 'I will not acquit the guilty,' Exodus 23:7, and Proverbs 17:15 calls acquitting the guilty detestable. That is why Paul's later claim that God 'justifies the wicked,' Romans 4:5, is so startling. The Greek behind 'no one' in verse 20 is 'no flesh,' pasa sarx ouk, the phrase from Psalm 143:2 and a reminder of human frailty. 'Awareness,' epignosis, is full knowledge, the word of 1:32, where the people 'know' God's decree and do the opposite. The law gives knowledge of what is wrong and no power to avoid it.

typology.type: God on trial and vindicated, Psalm 51:4 and Isaiah 5:3-4
typology.fulfillment: In Isaiah 5 God asks the people to 'judge between Me and My vineyard,' and in Micah 6:1-3 He argues a case against Israel. In Psalm 51 David confesses that God is right in His judgment. Paul's questions in verses 3 to 8 are the same trial in a new setting, with the verdict that God is true. The cross is the place where the trial reaches its end, since God shows there that He is shown 'just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:26. The pattern is a real correspondence, and it escalates in that God does not merely win the argument but takes the penalty upon Himself. It falls short in that Isaiah's vineyard was left to be destroyed, while the cross is where God's own Son bears the cost.

typology.type: Isaiah's unclean lips and the silenced mouth, Isaiah 6:5-7
typology.fulfillment: The catena speaks of throats like graves and lips with the venom of vipers. When Isaiah saw the LORD he cried, 'Woe is me, for I am ruined, because I am a man of unclean lips,' and an angel touched his mouth with a coal from the altar and said 'your iniquity is removed.' Isaiah is the person of verse 19 whose mouth is stopped and the person of verse 24 who is justified freely. The typology is a pattern of experience and not a prediction: the sinner is silenced before God, and then cleansed at the altar. It escalates in Christ, whose sacrifice is the altar's reality, and whose people can say with confidence, 'Who will bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies,' Romans 8:33.

Every mouth in the world is stopped by the evidence, but one Man stood accused and said nothing. 'He did not open His mouth,' Isaiah 53:7, and at His trial 'Jesus remained silent and made no reply,' Mark 14:61. The silence of the guilty and the silence of the Servant are different silences. The sinner is silent because he has no defense, and Jesus is silent because He has taken the guilt that others cannot answer for. The parallel is one of contrast, and Paul does not himself draw it, so it should be held as a reading and not as an explicit New Testament teaching.

typology.type: The corrupt flesh before the flood, Genesis 6:12
typology.fulfillment: The Hebrew of Genesis 6:12 says that 'all flesh' had corrupted its way, where the BSB reads 'all living creatures.' Paul's wording at the end of verse 20, that no flesh will be justified, uses the same word for human beings in their frailty. The flood generation gives a picture of a world where the verdict is universal, and Noah finds favor only by grace, Genesis 6:8. The type is a pattern of universal guilt answered by grace to one household. It escalates in Christ, through whom the grace is offered to every nation, and it falls short because the flood preserved a family while the gospel gives a new creation.

study.christ:
This passage prepares for Christ by showing what He is needed for, and each part of the argument turns toward Him.

The first is the faithfulness of God. Paul asks whether human unbelief can cancel God's faithfulness and answers that it cannot. The place where that answer is carried out is the Son. Paul writes that 'all the promises of God are Yes in Christ,' 2 Corinthians 1:20, and in Romans 15:8 that 'Christ has become a servant of the circumcised on behalf of God's truth, to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs.' The words that were entrusted to Israel, verse 2, find their fulfillment in the Word who became flesh, John 1:14. Jesus said, 'Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms,' Luke 24:44, and the Psalms and the Prophet Isaiah in the catena are among the texts in view.

The second is the question about God's justice. Paul's objector asks whether God can be just in judging a world whose sin serves His glory, and Paul simply denies it. He gives the full answer five verses later. At the cross God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice 'in order to demonstrate His righteousness, because in His forbearance He had passed over the sins committed beforehand,' and He did so 'so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:25-26. The objection of verses 5 to 8 supposes a God who can only be just by punishing or merciful by ignoring sin. The cross shows Him doing both at once. David's prayer in Psalm 51:4, that God be proved right when He judges, is answered at Calvary, where the judgment falls on the Judge's own Son.

The third is the verdict on humanity. The Old Testament portrait of the unrighteous is set against the one man of whom it can be said that He is the Righteous One. Peter says to the crowd, 'You rejected the Holy and Righteous One,' Acts 3:14, and John writes, 'we have an advocate before the Father, Jesus Christ, the Righteous One,' 1 John 2:1. The line 'there is no one righteous' receives its single exception, and the exception acts for others: 'Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God,' 1 Peter 3:18. In 2 Corinthians 5:21 the exchange is stated plainly, 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.'

The fourth is the stopped mouth. Everyone is silenced before the law. After 'But now,' the silence becomes the beginning of praise. The Psalm that says no one seeks God also asks for 'the salvation of Israel' to come from Zion, Psalm 14:7, and Isaiah 59 speaks of a Redeemer who comes after finding no one else to intercede, Isaiah 59:16-20. Paul recognizes the Redeemer in Christ in Romans 11:26. The very chapter from which he takes the diagnosis in verses 15 to 17 contains the promise of the cure.

A caution applies. The passage does not mention Jesus, and it is tempting to read every phrase as a hidden Christ. The links above depend on Paul's own use of the same texts and on the way his argument moves to the next verses. The proper reading is that the darkness of 3:9 to 20 has a purpose: it clears the ground so that the gift of 3:24, 'justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,' is received as a gift.
study.god:
The God of this passage is faithful, and Paul states it with unusual force. 'Let God be true and every man a liar,' verse 4, puts God's reliability on one side of a scale and the whole human race on the other. Numbers 23:19 says He is not a man that He should lie, and 2 Timothy 2:13 says that 'if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.' His faithfulness is not a response to ours. It is an expression of who He is, and it is the ground on which any human faith stands.

He is also a God who entrusts. Verse 2 says that Israel was given His own words. The Creator did not keep His speech to Himself. He placed it into human hands, knowing the hands would sometimes fail, and the verse treats the entrusting as an honor. The God of the Bible gives His word to people, and hearing it carries responsibility. Deuteronomy 4:7-8 speaks of a God near enough to be called on and of laws that are righteous, and the nearness is a gift that makes a claim.

He is the Judge of the world, and Paul accepts the logic of Abraham's question, 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?' Genesis 18:25. Verse 6 states that if God were not just He could not judge the world, and that if He did not judge the world He would not be God. The reality of judgment is a necessary part of His goodness. A God who overlooked evil would not be worthy of trust. The objection that sin may serve His glory is dismissed because it asks God to be judged by a standard lower than His own.

He exposes sin through His law. The law's work in verse 20, to bring awareness of sin, is not a failure of the law, which Paul calls 'holy, righteous, and good' in 7:12. It is the work of a physician who shows the sickness. Galatians 3:24 calls the law 'our guardian to lead us to Christ.' God is not sending people through a cruel hoop. He is showing the truth that must be seen before the cure can be welcomed.

He is a God who does not acquit the guilty without a ransom. Exodus 23:7 says He will not acquit the guilty, and Proverbs 17:15 calls it detestable. The word of Romans 3:19-20 means that no human defense will succeed, and there the weight of the argument falls. Whatever acquittal comes will have to come at His own expense, and that is exactly what the next verses announce.

For worship, the passage teaches silence and then song. The silence is that of Job, who said 'I place my hand over my mouth,' Job 40:4, before a God who asks the questions. The song follows, for the God who stops every mouth in verse 19 is the God who opens them again with praise, because He has been true to His promise in the Son.

crossReferences.note: David confesses that God is proved right when He speaks and blameless when He judges. Paul quotes it in verse 4 to show that God is vindicated even when human sin seems to magnify His glory. It is the voice of a guilty man who has been shown that God's verdict is true.

The main source of the catena. It describes the LORD looking down to see if any seek Him and finding that all have turned away. It ends with a longing for salvation from Zion, so the psalm itself moves from diagnosis to hope, which Paul will take up from 3:21.

Throats like open graves and tongues that practice deceit are the first line of verse 13. The psalm is a prayer against enemies who speak lies. Paul applies it to the human race, which shows that the portrait of the wicked in the Psalms is a mirror that includes the reader.

The venom of vipers on the lips supplies the second part of verse 13. The psalmist asks to be rescued from violent men, and Paul uses the image to describe how speech, the most ordinary human act, can be a weapon.

A mouth full of cursing, deceit and violence is the source of verse 14. The psalm complains that the wicked say in their hearts that God has forgotten, which links the catena to the denial of God at its root.

Feet swift to shed blood and the way of peace unknown are the text of verses 15 to 17. In the same chapter God sees there is no one to intercede, so His own arm brings salvation, Isaiah 59:16, which is the hope that the rest of Romans fulfills.

The oracle of transgression that ends 'There is no fear of God before his eyes' closes the catena in verse 18. The fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, Proverbs 9:10, so the portrait ends on the missing foundation of everything that went wrong.

Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins. The wisdom tradition makes the same claim as verse 10, so the verdict does not rest on the Psalms alone but on the Law, the Prophets and the Writings together.

The psalmist asks God not to bring His servant into judgment, for no one alive is righteous before Him. Paul draws on it in verse 20, with 'works of the law' added, and the prayer shows that a believer in the Old Testament already knew he could not stand on his record.

If a law could impart life, righteousness would come from it, but the law became a guardian to lead us to Christ. This is the positive side of Romans 3:20: the law that silences the mouth is meant to send the person to Christ and to justification by faith, not to a dead end.

God presents Christ as the atoning sacrifice to demonstrate His righteousness, passing over earlier sins in His forbearance, so as to be just and to justify. This is the answer to the objection of verses 5 and 6, and it shows that the questions of the passage are resolved at the cross.

The LORD saw that there was no one to intercede, so His own arm brought salvation, and a Redeemer would come to Zion. It is the cure that follows the diagnosis Paul quotes from the same chapter, and Romans 11:26 draws on it.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's account of humanity has an unusual shape. It begins with a very good creation, moves quickly to a fall, and then spends most of its pages on a God who keeps working with a people who keep failing. Romans 3:9 to 20 is the point at which that record is summed up in a single verdict. The line 'there is no one righteous' echoes the observation of Genesis 6:5 that the thoughts of the human heart were evil continually, and it anticipates the prayer of Psalm 130:3, 'If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand?' The answer implied in that psalm is that no one could.

The verdict also marks a turn in the story. Israel was the people through whom God meant to bless the world, and Paul's first question concerns their place. His answer is that they have the great advantage of the words of God, and that it has not made them better than the others. The Law was given to a people already in need, Romans 5:20. It increased the knowledge of sin, so that grace might increase all the more. Nothing in the failure of Israel catches God by surprise, and nothing in it cancels His promise.

The universal scope of the verdict is what opens the story outward. If Jew and Gentile are equally under sin, then the remedy must reach both. That is the logic of the whole letter, and of the whole movement from Abraham to the nations. Galatians 3:22 says Scripture confined all things under sin 'so that by faith in Jesus Christ the promise might be given to those who believe.' The word 'all' of this chapter is the ground for the 'all who believe' of the next.

The turning point comes in a few words. Verse 21 begins 'But now,' and the story moves from the courtroom to the cross. A Judge who knows that no one is righteous provides righteousness, and the God whose faithfulness cannot be cancelled keeps His promise in a way that no objector could have guessed. The church is then the community of people whose mouths were stopped and then opened, who confess sin and receive pardon.

In the new creation the verdict is reversed. The people who once had throats like open graves sing before the throne, Revelation 7:9-10. 'No one righteous' becomes a multitude clothed in white, with robes made white 'in the blood of the Lamb,' Revelation 7:14. The feet that were swift to shed blood walk in the light of the city, Revelation 21:24, and the eyes that had no fear of God 'will see His face,' Revelation 22:4. What the law could only expose, the gospel completes, and the God who judged the world in Romans 3 dwells with it in Revelation 21:3.

quiz.q: What does Paul name as the chief advantage of being a Jew?

options.text: They were entrusted with the very words, the oracles, of God.
options.note: Verse 2 says first of all they were entrusted with the very words of God.

options.text: They received and were made stewards of God's revelation.
options.note: Correct in substance; the text specifies this as the oracles or words of God.

options.text: They were guaranteed salvation by their descent from Abraham.
options.note: Descent gives no guarantee; Paul has just shown covenant privilege cannot save the disobedient.

options.text: They had no real advantage over the Gentiles at all.
options.note: Paul answers much in every way; the advantage is real, beginning with the oracles of God.

quiz.q: Does human unfaithfulness cancel God's faithfulness?

options.text: Certainly not; let God be true and every man a liar.
options.note: Verses 3 and 4 exactly: human unbelief cannot nullify God's faithfulness.

options.text: No; God stays reliable to His word even when people fail.
options.note: Right in meaning; Paul puts it as let God be true and every man a liar.

options.text: God's faithfulness partly depends on how His people respond.
options.note: Paul denies this; God's faithfulness does not rest on human faithfulness.

options.text: Yes; if people are unfaithful, God's promises fall to the ground.
options.note: Certainly not, says Paul; God remains true though every man is a liar.

quiz.q: What is the summary verdict of the Scripture chain in verses 10 to 18?

options.text: There is no one righteous, not even one; all have turned away.
options.note: The catena opens and hinges on this universal verdict.

options.text: Every person falls short and none seeks after God on his own.
options.note: Faithful to the sense; the text's sharp refrain is no one righteous, not even one.

options.text: Only the Gentiles are under sin, while Israel is exempt.
options.note: Paul insists Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin, not the Gentiles alone.

options.text: Most people are basically good with only occasional faults.
options.note: The catena declares the opposite: none is righteous, no not one.

quiz.q: Why does the law speak its verdict, according to verse 19?

options.text: So that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God.
options.note: Verse 19 states this purpose word for word.

options.text: So that all human boasting is stopped and everyone stands guilty before God.
options.note: Correct in meaning; the text speaks of every mouth silenced and the world accountable.

options.text: So that those under the law can earn acquittal by keeping it.
options.note: The reverse; verse 20 says no one is justified by works of the law.

options.text: So that the Gentiles alone are shown to be sinners.
options.note: The law silences every mouth and holds the whole world, not only Gentiles, accountable.

quiz.q: What does the law accomplish regarding justification, according to verse 20?

options.text: By works of the law no one is justified; the law brings knowledge of sin.
options.note: Verse 20 says exactly this: no justification by works, only awareness of sin.

options.text: The law cannot make anyone righteous; it only reveals their sin.
options.note: Right in substance; the text specifies no one is justified by works of the law.

options.text: The law justifies those who try their sincere best to keep it.
options.note: Paul denies this; sincere effort at law keeping cannot justify anyone.

options.text: The law removes sin from those who study it carefully.
options.note: The law brings awareness of sin; it has no power to remove it.

questions: Israel's great privilege was being entrusted with the words of God. How seriously do you treat the privilege of possessing the Scriptures, and does that privilege lead you to trust or to presume?
Paul insists that God stays faithful even when people are faithless. Where do you need to rest in God's reliability rather than in your own consistency?
Scripture declares there is no one righteous, not even one. How does an honest reckoning with your own sin, rather than comparing yourself to others, change how you see your need for grace?
Paul says every mouth is stopped before God. What excuses or self-justifications do you still bring before God that this passage silences?
The law can diagnose sin but cannot cure it. How does recognizing what the law cannot do sharpen your longing for the righteousness that comes through Christ?

translationNotes.note: The very words of God renders ta logia, which some translations give as the oracles of God. It refers to the whole of God's revelation entrusted to Israel, a stewardship rather than a boast.
So that You may be proved right when You speak quotes Psalm 51:4. The point is that God is vindicated, shown to be in the right, even and especially in His judgments.

Works of the law refers to deeds done in obedience to the Mosaic law. Paul's point, recovered by the Reformers, is that no such works can justify; the law's role is to bring awareness of sin, not acceptance with God.
